bib.title: Principled Instructions Are All You Need for Questioning LLaMA-1/2, GPT-3.5/4

read.skipped: Heatmap cell numbers in Figs 10-12 are present as loose numbers; row/column order is ambiguous in the text layer so they were not recorded.

question: Do 26 hand-written prompting principles improve response quality and correctness across LLaMA-1/2 (7B-70B), GPT-3.5 and GPT-4?
hypothesis: Better-crafted prompts following the principles yield higher-quality, more concise, factual responses, and larger models benefit more (stated as a finding, not a prior).
contributions: 26 guiding principles for prompting, grouped into five categories (Tables 1-2)
Experiments on LLaMA-1/2 (7B, 13B, 70B), GPT-3.5/4 with the manually built ATLAS benchmark

method.summary: The authors wrote 26 prompt principles and compared each pair of responses to the same question with and without a principle applied, judged by humans, on seven models. Two measures: boosting (quality gain, simple tasks) and correctness (absolute and relative, reasoning tasks).
method.task: prompt design evaluation (human side-by-side judging of LLM responses)

datasets.name: ATLAS
datasets.size: 20 human-selected questions per principle, plus 20 for the challenging subset
datasets.split: standard subset (questions across domains) and challenging subset (reasoning and other complex tasks); each question asked with and without the principled prompt
datasets.source: manually crafted benchmark, cited as Shen, Bsharat, Myrzakhan, ATLAS, preprint 2024

inference.samples: a single response for each question, with and without the principle; no repeats or seeds stated
inference.prompting: Each principle applied to the question text (e.g. few-shot examples for principle 7, 'let's think step by step' for 12, a hint or 'Explanation :' primer for 20). For correctness, principles 14, 15, 21, 22, 23 are not applicable and are skipped.

parameters.scale_groups: small = 7B models, medium = 13B, large = 70B and GPT-3.5/4

metrics.name: Boosting
metrics.definition: percentage increase in response quality across a set of questions when the principles are applied, by human evaluation, with the unmodified prompt as the baseline; simpler tasks

metrics.name: Absolute correctness
metrics.definition: accuracy of the model's responses on complex reasoning questions with the principle, by human evaluators

metrics.name: Relative correctness improvement
metrics.definition: improvement in correctness accuracy over the unmodified prompt (exact formula not given)

baselines: same question without the principle (original prompt)
eval.protocol: Human evaluation of paired responses, in the manner of AlpacaEval and MT-Bench; number of raters, rater agreement, instructions, blinding and significance tests not stated.

availability.data: ATLAS at the project page above (stated as project page)

prompts.text: Add "I'm going to tip $xxx for a better solution!"
Use leading words like writing "think step by step".

If you prefer more concise answers, no need to be polite with LLM so there is no need to add phrases like "please", "if you don't mind", "thank you", "I would like to", etc., and get straight to the point.
Ensure that your answer is unbiased and avoids relying on stereotypes.

evidence.quote: of responses from the same instructions with and without principles

results.claim: Principled prompts raised GPT-4 response quality by 57.7% and accuracy by 36.4% on average on ATLAS.
results.setup: ATLAS, GPT-4, human evaluation, single response per question, average over principles
results.quote: enhanced both the quality and accuracy of the LLM responses by an average of 57.7% and 36.4%, respectively, when applied to GPT-4
results.note: The text does not say which of Figs 7-9 gives these two numbers or how accuracy is averaged.

results.claim: Gains grow with model size; going from LLaMA-2-7B to GPT-4 the gain exceeds 20%.
results.quote: the performance gains when moving from LLaMA-2-7B to GPT-4 exceed 20%

results.claim: Boosting is about 50% on average across LLMs.
results.quote: On average, there is a stable 50% improvement across different LLMs.

results.claim: Models reach only 20-40% average absolute correctness, large models above 40%.
results.setup: ATLAS reasoning questions with principles applied, Fig 5 averaged over principles
results.quote: Generally, these models achieve 20%∼40% accuracy on the averaged performance

results.claim: Relative correctness improves by over 10% on average, and can exceed 20% for larger models.
results.quote: Fig. 6 illustrates that applying the principles generally leads to a performance increase of over 10% across different models on average.

results.claim: Correctness improvement rises with model size from LLaMA-2-13B through GPT-4.
results.note: qualitative: 'the larger the model, the greater the increase in correctness improvement'

results.claim: Principle 14 improved every question it was applied to.
results.note: qualitative: 'for principle 14, as shown in Fig. 4, it has improved all questions it is applied to'

limits: Authors concede effectiveness may diminish on very complex or highly specialized questions.
Only seven models tested; other architectures may respond differently.
Assessment rests on a limited selection of questions (20 per principle); criteria and results may vary across human assessors.
No rater count, agreement, decoding settings, or significance tests; one response per question, so scores move in 5-point steps (inferred from 20 questions).

Principles were tested one at a time against a baseline; no interaction or ablation study; the prompt wording changes beyond the principle are not controlled (e.g. Fig 2 also rewords 'short' to 'small').

terms.definition: the percentage increase in response quality across a set of questions when the proposed principles are applied
the precision of the model's outputs or responses, ensuring they are accurate, relevant, and devoid of errors
